title: Why make a world?
hookLine: if God needs nothing, why make a world at all? the Brahma Sutra's answer is one word: lila, play
carry: lila: the world made from fullness, as play

lines: IF GOD HAS EVERYTHING, WHY MAKE ANYTHING?
cards: A child's question, and a philosopher's too: if God already has everything, why make anything? People act because they lack something.
They cook because they're hungry, work because the rent is due, build because the roof leaks. A being who lacks nothing has no reason to lift a finger.

So either God needed the world, which would mean God wasn't complete, or the world has no reason at all. The Brahma Sutra raises this objection itself, plainly, as a problem for anyone who says Brahman made the world.
Then it answers in a handful of words, and on this last day with the Sri Bhashya, Ramanuja unpacks them.

teach.h: ONLY PLAY, AS IN THE WORLD.
teach.b: The sutra's answer: it is only lila, play, as in the world. Ramanuja gives the picture.
A great king who already rules everything, who wants for nothing, still plays a game with a ball, just for the joy of it. Nobody says he's playing because he's short of something.
So too, he says, the Lord brings forth the world, holds it up and draws it back, as play: not from need, but from fullness.
For Ramanuja the world is real, and it's held close: the world and every self are like the Lord's body, as yesterday's lesson put it. So this play isn't a trick or a dream.

It's real, it's close, and it rests in someone who is joy itself. It's also why Hindus call the stories of Krishna and Rama lila, and why towns act out the Ram Lila every autumn: God's play, retold as ours.
Look back across the week with him. Brahman as a person. Without qualities read as without faults.
Knowing as a thread of oil that becomes love. The atman, a lamp and its light. Moksha, a self freed into its own shine.
And today, a world made from fullness, as play. That's Vaishnava theology in a few strokes: careful argument, all of it in service of a God the Alvars sang to.
Next, the same Brahma Sutras open again, read through another great commentator, Shankara, with jnana, knowing, at the center.

how: Sri Vaishnavas speak of creation as the Lord's lila, his play, and celebrate it in festivals and stories of Vishnu's descents; students meet the argument in the Sri Bhashya's comment on the Brahma Sutra's second chapter.

o: the order of chants used in Vishnu's temple rites
careful reasoning about Vishnu, selves and the world
the life stories of the Alvar saints, told in order

games.q: a world made as play: tap the pairs.
p: a God who needs nothing has no reason to act
real, and held close like a body

s: for Ramanuja, God made the world because he needed something
the world comes from fullness, as play, the way a king who lacks nothing plays ball.
the Brahma Sutra raises the objection about God's motive itself
then answers: it is only play, as in the world.
calling the world play means, for Ramanuja, the world isn't real
for him the world is real, and held close like the Lord's body.

games.q: someone objects: a God who needs nothing has no reason to make a world. you're Ramanuja. how do you answer?
o: then God must have needed the world after all.
then the world can't really exist.
it's play, like a king with everything who still plays a game.
games.why: following the Brahma Sutra, Ramanuja says creation is lila: play that comes from fullness, not need.

practice: Notice how much of today has run on lack: something to fix, something to get, something to finish, and let that be there.
Then, for a few breaths, notice what's already enough: the breath arriving on its own, the floor holding you, light in the room.
Let the breath move as if it were play, not work; if you pray, rest in the name you pray to, and in the world held close.

wordCard.voice: Vaishnava theology. Today, lila: a world made not from need but from fullness, as play, real and held close by the Lord.

orig.note: Sanskrit: play, the Brahma Sutra's word for why the Lord brings forth the world.

carryVoice: Your line: lila: the world made from fullness, as play. A king plays ball, not because he lacks, but because he's full. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Brahma Sutra 2.1.32–33 (not, because of having a motive; but it is mere play, as in the world)
